shared_context.chief_complaint: Fatigue and dark urine for 1 day
shared_context.medical_history: Recently diagnosed cellulitis of the left leg; no significant past medical history
shared_context.medications: Recently prescribed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; no other current medications
shared_context.vitals: Temperature 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure 115/72 mmHg, pulse 98/min, respirations 14/min
shared_context.labs: Hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 470 U/L, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase 7 U/gHb (normal 6-20 U/gHb)

atoms.1: Fatigue, dark urine, and conjunctival icterus suggest hemolytic anemia.
atoms.2: Elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels are consistent with hemolysis.
atoms.3: The direct bilirubin level is elevated.
atoms.4: Elevated direct bilirubin level indicates that the jaundice is due to direct (conjugated) bilirubin.
atoms.5: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin is produced when hemoglobin is broken down.
atoms.6: A hemoglobin level of 7.2 g/dL further supports the diagnosis of hemolytic anemia.
atoms.7: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can cause hemolysis in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.
atoms.8: An elevated G6PD level of 7 U/gHb suggests that the patient has G6PD deficiency.
atoms.9: Considering the patient's symptoms and laboratory results, the most likely finding on a peripheral blood smear would be spherocytes.
atoms.10: Spherocytes are erythrocytes that have lost their biconcave disk shape.
atoms.11: Spherocytes appear as smooth, round cells.
atoms.12: Spherocytes are a common finding in hemolytic anemia caused by G6PD deficiency.

snippets.output: Fatigue, dark urine, and conjunctival icterus suggest hemolytic anemia. Elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels are consistent with hemolysis. A hemoglobin level of 7.2 g/dL further supports the diagnosis of hemolytic anemia.
The direct bilirubin level is elevated, indicating that the jaundice is due to direct (conjugated) bilirubin, which is produced when hemoglobin is broken down.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can cause hemolysis in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.
An elevated G6PD level of 7 U/gHb does not suggest G6PD deficiency.
Spherocytes are erythrocytes that have lost their biconcave disk shape and appear as smooth, round cells.
Spherocytes are not a common finding in hemolytic anemia caused by G6PD deficiency.
Considering the patient's symptoms and laboratory results, the most likely finding on a peripheral blood smear would not be spherocytes.
